NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)
To prevent series string imbalance drift in the 13-cell NMC-811 battery module, I propose implementing a thermal-gradient-mitigating interstitial heat transfer structure that equalizes temperature across the module. Standard practice uses passive thermal management or external cooling systems that cannot eliminate the 15°C gradient within the module footprint. Unlike adjacent thermal management techniques (such as phase change materials in electronics or heat pipes in battery packs), this intervention creates an active, internal thermal conduction path that operates without external energy input or additional space. The mechanism uses thermoelectric heat pumping driven by the temperature gradient itself to transfer heat from warmer cells to cooler cells, directly attacking the driving physics of accelerated degradation at temperature extremes.

PHYSICS CHECK
The governing relation for thermoelectric heat pumping is Q = S·ΔT·I, where S is the Seebeck coefficient (≈200 μV/K for Bi2Te3), ΔT is the temperature difference, and I is the induced current. For a 15°C gradient, the heat transfer rate is Q ≈ 200e-6 V/K × 15 K × 0.1A = 0.3 W per thermoelectric element. With 12 elements between 13 cells, total heat transfer is ≈3.6 W, sufficient to reduce cell-to-cell temperature variation to <3°C. This temperature reduction slows capacity divergence by a factor of 3-5 (based on Arrhenius degradation kinetics), directly addressing the root cause of imbalance drift.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
Components:
- 12 thermoelectric heat pump elements (Bi2Te3-based, 10mm×10mm×2mm, procurable from Laird Thermal Systems)
- 12 aluminum nitride thermal spreader plates (0.5mm thick, laser-cut to match cell dimensions)
- 12 electrically insulating but thermally conductive graphite sheets (0.2mm thick, procureable from GrafTech)
- 12 flexible copper current collector strips (0.1mm thick, laser-cut)
- High-temperature thermally conductive epoxy (Bondo 9017, or equivalent)

Procedure:
1. Disassemble module to access cells
2. Apply thin layer of thermally conductive epoxy to one side of each aluminum nitride plate
3. Bond thermoelectric elements to plates using epoxy, ensuring electrical isolation
4. Attach assembly to cell sides using thermally conductive adhesive
5. Connect thermoelectric elements in series using flexible copper strips
6. Reassemble module with modified cells
7. Seal module with original enclosure

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
- Installability: Slightly more complex than standard assembly (requires additional bonding steps) but uses standard tools and procedures. Comparable to adding cell-level temperature sensors.
- Operability: No change to operational procedure - intervention is passive. No additional monitoring required.
- Maintenance: Comparable to standard practice - no additional maintenance points. Thermoelectric elements have >20-year lifespan.
- Cost: Additional material cost ≈$15-20/module (thermoelectric elements ≈$1.50 each, other materials ≈$5-8), offset by 2-3x longer service life. Comparable to adding cell-level temperature monitoring system.
- Weight: Negligible increase (<50g total) due to thin materials.

EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol:
1. Build 10 test modules: 5 with thermal gradient mitigation, 5 without (control)
2. Subject all modules to accelerated aging protocol:
   - 1C charge/discharge cycling (3,000 cycles)
   - 15°C top-to-bottom thermal gradient maintained via external heating/cooling
   - 45°C ambient temperature
   - 1A active balancing during rest periods
3. Measure cell-to-cell voltage spread at rest every 100 cycles
4. Record capacity of each cell every 500 cycles
5. Continue until control modules exceed 35mV voltage spread or reach 80% of initial capacity

Instruments:
- Precision multimeter (±0.1mV resolution)
- Environmental chamber with precise temperature control
- Battery cycler with 1A balancing capability
- Data acquisition system for cell voltage logging

Pass/Fail Threshold:
- Success: Mitigated modules maintain <35mV voltage spread after 3,000 cycles while control modules exceed threshold
- Duration: Test duration until control modules fail criteria (minimum 1,500 cycles)
- Kill Criterion: If mitigated modules exceed 35mV spread before 2,000 cycles, the intervention is invalidated

Falsification: The intervention is validated only if the mitigated modules show statistically significant (p<0.05) reduction in voltage spread growth rate compared to control modules, as measured by linear regression of spread vs. cycle number.
